analysis.one_liner: Taxes every stock, bond, and derivatives trade at 0.1 percent.
analysis.headline: The bill got no hearing and no vote: with 21 supporters in the House, all Democrats, it sat in the Ways and Means Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a 0.1 percent tax on each purchase of stocks, bonds, and derivatives traded in the U.S. or by U.S. persons, with initial issues and very short-term debt exempt. The tax is collected by exchanges and brokers, so investors would barely notice it, but high-frequency traders and large financial firms executing huge numbers of trades would pay substantially. It never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The general public, if the new revenue is used for public purposes; the tax is designed so buy-and-hold investors pay almost nothing while frequent, high-volume traders pay the most.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers, via a new revenue stream

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 0.1 percent excise tax on purchases of stocks, bonds, and derivatives traded on U.S. exchanges or by U.S. persons [S2][S3]
Exempts initial issuances of securities and short-term debt with maturities of 100 days or less, sparing much routine business financing [S2][S3]

Collected by exchanges and brokers rather than billed to individual investors, and applies to controlled foreign corporations with U.S. shareholders to limit avoidance by shifting trades offshore [S3]

analysis.who_pays: High-frequency trading firms, banks, hedge funds, and other large financial institutions whose profits depend on enormous numbers of trades; retirement savers would bear only a trivial cost on infrequent trades but funds would bear collection paperwork.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wall Street trading firms and banks

drawbacks.text: The tax applies to every covered trade, including purchases inside mutual funds and retirement accounts when they rebalance, so some of the cost would reach ordinary investors through slightly higher fund expenses [S3]

The bill directs the Treasury Secretary to write rules to prevent avoidance, including the use of non-U.S. persons in transactions, an implicit acknowledgment that some trading could move to foreign venues to escape the tax [S3]

Because the tax is levied per transaction, its burden falls most heavily on exactly the trading activity that also supplies market liquidity, an effect critics of financial transaction taxes generally emphasize [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A 0.1 percent rate is small enough that long-term savers would pay almost nothing, while the concentrated cost lands on high-volume traders whose activity contributes little to household wealth-building. The main honest concerns are that some trading could migrate abroad and that fund investors would bear a sliver of the tax plus compliance costs. On balance the design targets speculation rather than saving, though its revenue would depend on how much trading stayed onshore.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never held a hearing or markup, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Val Hoyle introduced the bill on July 25, 2023, joined by 18 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S3]
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S5]
No further action was ever taken: the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5]
The bill ended with 20 cosponsors, all House Democrats, and no Republican support [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-frequency trading firms, banks, and other large financial institutions avoided a new tax on their trading volume, and the Republican chair of Ways and Means avoided a vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it [S4][S5].

industries.industry: High-frequency and high-volume securities traders (banks, hedge funds, proprietary trading firms)
industries.note: These firms execute enormous numbers of trades at thin margins, so even 0.1 percent per transaction would take a meaningful bite out of their profits. Avoiding the tax preserved the current cost structure of high-volume trading.

Exchanges and brokers would have become the tax collectors under the bill, adding compliance duties, while a per-trade tax could reduce trading volumes on their venues. Ordinary investors transact through these venues and would feel any volume shift indirectly.
Fund trades in stocks and bonds would be taxed, raising fund expenses slightly for savers, and funds would handle collection and reporting on transactions inside retirement accounts.
